html:
Whereas Predicted Particle Spectra derived the symbolic spectral laws governing elementary fermions, composite hadrons, atomic shells, and nuclear decay rates across the archimedean realization \tau_{\mathrm{arch}}, this chapter serves as the unified experimental scorecard of the framework. Evaluating every symbolic invariant at the calibrated substrate modulus q_0 \approx 1.1100, it confronts the predictions with CODATA 2022, PDG 2024, and AME 2020 precision benchmarks and formulates concrete, falsifiable experimental protocols.

Along the five-step categorical pipeline (Category -> Hecke/Markov Algebra -> Hyperbolic/Bring Geometry -> Archimedean Period Realization -> Physical Spectra), the empirical verification is organized into six stages:

  1. The substrate consistency window and three-calibration discipline: Independent physical observables—charged-lepton mass ratios, the fine-structure constant \alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}^{-1}, nucleon mass ratios, and nuclear \beta-decay Q-values—each invert to determine the substrate modulus q_0, converging within a narrow consistency window around q_0 \approx 1.10997858 under the strict three-anchor discipline (\mathrm{CAL\text{-}1}\;m_e, \mathrm{CAL\text{-}2}\;q_0, \mathrm{CAL\text{-}3}\;m_\pi).
  2. Particle identification tests and two-mode double-slit interferometry: Topological assignments for the Borromean quark core, the T(2,8) Higgs link and electroweak vacuum expectation value, and S_5-equivariant torus knots are paired with the q-deformed double-slit diffraction predictions for massive particles versus photons.
  3. Lepton, hadron, electroweak, and nuclear mass comparisons: Calibrating q_0 from the lepton sector yields zero-parameter predictions for the proton and neutron masses, the neutron–proton mass difference m_n - m_p, light atomic masses (1 \le Z \le 20), and the W-boson mass.
  4. Beta-decay half-lives, magic-shell closures, and Strutinsky residues: Across twenty orders of magnitude in weak decay lifetimes, the imaginary complex-volume component \mathfrak{Q}_\beta = \operatorname{Im}\mathfrak{V}, the N_V brane-tower depth, and diagrammatic Littlewood–Richardson fusion confront measured half-lives and magic numbers \{2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126\}.
  5. Extreme-density strangelet phase transitions and precision laboratory protocols: The Borromean-to-Hopf diquark crossover in neutron-star cores, the photonic quantum Hall effect, the muonic proton-radius shift, crystal Bragg-resonance shifts, and Breit–Wheeler pair creation provide targeted laboratory and astrophysical falsifiability tests.
  6. Non-commutative probability, the q-Central Limit Theorem, and interactive simulators: The GNS construction on the inductive-limit Hecke algebra H_\infty(q) under the Markov trace at z = q^3/(q^2+1) establishes the macroscopic q-Gaussian limit and anchors the chapter's interactive numerical simulators.

Conventions on numerical comparisons and units. Plain italic symbols m_e, m_p, m_n denote the CODATA-measured electron, proton, and neutron rest masses, whereas Gothic \mathfrak{m}(K) = \mathrm{Vol}(K)/\hbar_q^2 denotes the dimensionless categorical mass functional. Because m_e fixes the overall MeV energy unit by calibration (\mathrm{CAL\text{-}1}), the predictive content of every mass entry is the dimensionless ratio \mathfrak{m}(K)/\mathfrak{m}(4_1), which is rendered in MeV by multiplying by m_e. Numerical evaluations at q_0 are written with \approx to distinguish archimedean decimal evaluations from exact algebraic identities over \mathbb{Q}(q).
